reading.rtitle: No New Facts, One Last Chance
paras: A closing argument is the only speech in a negotiation where nothing you say is new. Everything has been said already, by both sides, and the room has heard all of it. What is left to choose is the order and the weight: which sentence goes first, which fact is allowed to carry the ending, and what the room is looking at when you stop talking. Not once in the whole history of mediation has a case been won by the person who simply repeated the most.

The advice most people are given is to open with their strongest point, and it is not quite right. What works better is to open with what nobody disputes, because it is the only sentence everybody in the room can accept, and agreement is easier to build on than resistance. Then comes the part that feels wrong and is not: concede your weakest point yourself, in the first minute, before the other side reaches it. A point conceded early costs almost nothing. The same point, taken from you, costs the room's trust in everything else you say.

The middle of the speech is where structure does the work. If somebody had read the clause in March, none of this would have happened is not an accusation; it says where it could have stopped without blaming anybody in particular. All she is asking for is one line on the copyright page tells the room exactly what to look at and, by leaving everything else out, what not to. Both sentences would be weaker as plain statements, and the difference is not decoration. It is the difference between being heard and being understood.

Then stop. Almost nobody regrets a closing argument that was too short, and everybody who has ever laboured a point has watched the room stop listening while they were still speaking. What people remember is rarely the argument itself; it is whether the person making it looked poised, and poise is a skill rather than a temperament. It comes from a plan short enough to read at a glance and from the willingness to wrap up before anybody expects it.

listenings.text: The last speech is the only one where you are not allowed to bring anything new, and that is the whole difficulty of it. Everything you could possibly say has already been said, by you or by the other side, and the room has heard all of it. So the only things left to choose are the order and the weight. Which sentence goes first, and what is the room looking at when you stop. The thing I spend most of my time arguing about with people I train is the weakest point. Everybody wants to leave it alone and hope. Concede it in the first minute, before the other side gets anywhere near it. A point you concede yourself costs you almost nothing. The same point taken from you costs the room's trust in every other thing you have said, and you never get that back inside ninety seconds. And about nerves, because somebody always asks. Poise is a skill, not a temperament. I have never met anybody who was not nervous. The two things that make a person look poised are a plan short enough to read at a glance, and being willing to stop talking early. That is it. Nobody has ever complained that a closing argument was too short.

Between my first mock mediation and my tenth, my vocabulary did not change at all. I want to be honest about that, because everybody assumes it must have. I knew almost exactly the same words on the first day as I did at the end, and I was just as nervous in the tenth as I was in the first. Nobody stops being nervous. What changed was that I stopped abandoning sentences halfway through. That was it, and I only noticed because somebody in the group was counting. In the first session I started and dropped eleven sentences in four minutes. Eleven. By the tenth it was two, and the two were on purpose, because I had thought of something better. Nobody who watched me would have said I had learned more English. They would have said I sounded like somebody who knew what he was doing. So when people come to me now and say they need more vocabulary before they can do this, I tell them what I wish somebody had told me. Almost nobody in my group needed more words. What they needed was to finish the sentence they had already started. That is a habit, not a level, and habits change in weeks.
